summary: Darwin's orchid is an epiphytic orchid endemic to Madagascar, where it usually grows on trees along lowland forest edges. Its waxy, star-shaped flowers release a powerful spicy scent only at night and carry nectar in spurs 27–43 cm long. That extraordinary structure led Charles Darwin in 1862 to predict a moth with a matching tongue; a suitable Madagascan moth was discovered in 1903, making the orchid a celebrated example in the history of evolutionary thought.

Panda plant is an evergreen succulent subshrub endemic to east-central Madagascar, where it grows on rocky, well-drained ground in seasonally dry country. Its thick leaves are covered in fine silvery hairs, giving them a felt-like surface, while dark brown or rusty markings edge the scalloped margins. The plant is widely grown for this distinctive foliage, although indoor specimens rarely produce its small tubular flowers.

Carolina fanwort is a rooted aquatic perennial native to parts of North and South America. Its stems grow through still or slow-moving water, with flowers floating at or rising above the surface. Long popular in aquariums, it has escaped cultivation around the world. Brittle late-summer stems break into fragments that help it spread, and vegetative reproduction appears to be its main route into new waters; it is now a regulated invasive plant in Australia and the European Union.

Euphorbia hirta is a hairy annual herb originating in the tropical Americas and now widespread through the tropics. It grows in open grassland, roadsides and paths, and may stand upright or trail along the ground. Its stems release abundant white latex, while tiny flowers and three-sided fruit capsules cluster closely at the leaf nodes. The plant has a long record of use in traditional herbal medicine across several cultures, including as a medicinal tea in the Philippines.

Avellinia festucoides is a herbaceous grass. It was first described in 1800 as Bromus festucoides and transferred to Avellinia in 2006. Its epithet means 'resembling Festuca,' referring to the plant's similarity in appearance to grasses in that genus.

Common peony is a herbaceous perennial native mainly to mountainous parts of southern Europe. It produces divided leaves and large, bowl-shaped deep-pink or deep-red flowers in late spring. The plant was first used medicinally and later became an ornamental, with many horticultural selections now grown even though the typical species is uncommon in cultivation. It also persists in the wild across Europe.

Rosa gallica is a deciduous rose native from southern and central Europe east to Turkey and the Caucasus. It forms broad patches and bears fragrant, deep-pink flowers, sometimes with doubled petals. Cultivated by Greeks and Romans and common in medieval gardens, it remained Europe's most important cultivated rose species until the 19th century. It also contributed ancestry to many modern European rose cultivars.

Galium viscosum is a flowering herb native to mainland Portugal and endemic to the southwestern Iberian Peninsula and northwestern Africa. It grows in fallow ground and traditional rain-fed olive groves on basic soils. A regional Portuguese assessment classified it as Vulnerable after finding a scattered population, a restricted occupied area and continuing declines in habitat and range, driven chiefly by the conversion of traditional olive groves to intensive agriculture.

Roseleaf sage is a herbaceous perennial native to Puebla, Tamaulipas and Veracruz in Mexico, where it grows in shaded places such as forest edges. Its name refers to the conspicuous bracts surrounding the flowers: pairs of beetroot-red bracts enclose groups of three blooms, then fall as the flowers expand. The species also crosses readily with other sages, and cultivated hybrids can show stronger growth and longer flowering periods.

Large-flowered pink-sorrel is a bulbous perennial originating in South America and now found on every continent except Antarctica. Its leaves have a sharp lemony flavour, and its flowers, leaves and roots are described as edible. In Europe it is sterile and spreads only through bulbs, while its seeds elsewhere can be flung from elastic fruit capsules. The plant can become troublesome enough that the Royal Horticultural Society calls it a serious weed.

summary: Aechmea recurvata is a plant species native to southern Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay and northern Argentina. Three botanical varieties are recognised across this range, including locally named varieties from Santa Catarina and São Paulo. The species is also widely cultivated as an ornamental and has given rise to numerous named cultivars and intergeneric hybrids.

Greater broomrape is a perennial parasitic plant native to Europe that lacks chlorophyll and depends entirely on other plants for nutrients. It attaches to the roots of shrubs in the bean family, especially common broom and European gorse, so it occurs only where suitable hosts grow. Above ground it forms a honey-brown, downy flower spike with scale-like leaves; after flowering, the spike persists as a dark brown stem containing minute seeds.

Cenizo is an evergreen shrub native to Texas and the northern Mexican states of Coahuila, Nuevo León and Tamaulipas. Despite the name Texas sage, it is not a true sage. Its abundant purple flowers and low water needs make it a widely planted ornamental in warm, dry regions, while its leaves feed caterpillars of the theona checkerspot and calleta silkmoth. Folklore says flowering predicts rain, though humidity or low pressure may trigger blooms before or after rainfall.

False olive is an evergreen shrub or small tree native to South Africa and Zimbabwe, occurring from coastal country to the central plateau, often in ravines and beside rock outcrops. Its narrow leaves are smooth and dark above but covered with pale star-shaped hairs beneath. Large heads of cream or white, honey-scented flowers appear in spring and summer. Its dense, high-quality timber is rarely available in pieces large enough for furniture.

Limonium lowei is a flowering plant in the family Plumbaginaceae, endemic to Madeira in Portugal. The species was formally published in 2007 and is not protected under Portuguese or European Community legislation according to the supplied account.

Festuca brigantina is a flowering grass. Its nominate subspecies, Festuca brigantina subsp. brigantina, occurs in mainland Portugal, where the supplied account describes it as endemic. That subspecies is protected under Annexes II and IV of the European Union's Habitats Directive.

Crepis lampsanoides is a flowering plant in the family Asteraceae, native to mainland Portugal. The supplied account states that it is not protected under Portuguese or European Community legislation.

Spanish lavender is a bushy evergreen shrub native to Iberia, Morocco and western Turkey. Narrow, aromatic grey-green leaves surround long-stalked heads of small dark-purple flowers. Two or three narrow, butterfly-like purple bracts rise from the top of each oval flower head, giving the species its most distinctive feature. Five subspecies are recognised across the plant's range.

Red vetchling is a hairless annual wild pea native to Europe, North Africa and the Middle East. It climbs with branched tendrils and produces single red flowers followed by smooth pods that split open. The species has a complicated food history: it was listed as cicerchia among foods enjoyed in Milan in 1288, yet the source also identifies it as one of the peas known to cause lathyrism.

summary: Silver squill is a bulbous perennial native to South Africa's Eastern Cape Province. First described in 1870 as Scilla socialis, it was transferred to Ledebouria in 1970 when the former genus was revised. The name socialis refers to its habit of growing in colonies or pure stands. It is also often cultivated and is described as thriving with little care.

Saw-toothed azara is an evergreen shrub endemic to Chile. It grows to about four metres, with glossy, serrated leaves and clusters of scented yellow flowers in summer. Its two recognised varieties divide the range between the Juan Fernández Islands and central to southern mainland Chile. In temperate climates the shrub needs a sheltered position.

Wild gladiolus is a flowering plant found in western and southern Europe, especially around the Mediterranean, and grows to about 50 cm tall. Britain has a small population in the New Forest, although one cited view suggests it may have been introduced there. The species received legal protection in the United Kingdom in 1975.
Madeira elder is a species of elderberry endemic to Madeira, the island in the eastern Atlantic Ocean. Its scientific description under the name Sambucus lanceolata was published in 1831.
Delphinium gracile is a flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae, native to the western Mediterranean. A diterpenoid alkaloid called graciline has been isolated from its tissues.
